Q8. 
PLEASE PROVIDE AN OVERVIEW OF THE CURRENT PJM OPEN-
2 
ACCESS TRANSMISSION TARIFF (“TARIFF”). 
3 
A8. 
The current tariff provides rates that are assessed to loads for transmission service, 
4 
ancillary services, energy, and capacity. The primary relevant service for which 
5 
loads take service is Network Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”). This 
6 
provides a mechanism for new load to interconnect to the transmission system and 
7 
purchase system energy. Loads are charged for transmission service based on their 
8 
contribution to their zone’s annual peak load, with specific calculation 
9 
methodologies that vary by transmission owner.11 Loads are charged for ancillary 
10 
services based on their monthly energy, monthly contribution to the zone’s annual 
11 
peak load, or monthly non-coincident peak demand depending on the specific 
12 
service.

Q9. 
WHAT 
RATE 
DESIGN 
PRINCIPLES 
ARE 
APPROPRIATE 
TO 
14 
CONSIDER IN THE DEVELOPMENT OF A TRANSMISSION TARIFF? 
15 
A9. 
The Bonbright rate design principles are well-established as the seminal standard 
16 
for establishing electric utility rates across North America.12 Underscoring their 
17 
relevance in PJM, FERC has cited these principles on numerous occasions.13 
18

single annual peak hour), 5 CP or 12 CP (average customer load over 5 or 12 annual peak hours).

Q10. WHICH SPECIFIC BONBRIGHT RATE DESIGN PRINCIPLES ARE 
1 
RELEVANT 
TO 
THE 
ISSUE 
OF 
CO-LOCATED 
LOAD 
AND 
2 
GENERATION? 
3 
A10. There are two rate design principles that are most relevant to the development of 
4 
tariffs for co-located load and generation: 
5 
• Fair apportionment of costs: this principle establishes that costs should be 
6 
borne by the customers that cause the costs. Fair apportionment of costs 
7 
drives equity among customers. 
8 
• Economic efficiency: this principle discourages wasteful infrastructure 
9 
development and use while promoting all justified types and amounts of 
10 
use. Application of this principle yields an electricity system that serves 
11 
load at minimum total cost.  
12 
 
13 
 
In addition, Bonbright also establishes that rates should be “free from 
14 
controversies as to improper interpretation” and “non-discriminatory.”14 Finally, 
15 
Bonbright also establishes several other principles that are less relevant to the topic 
16 
of co-located loads because all rate design proposals in this proceeding perform 
17 
similarly.15 For example, all rate options under consideration recover the total 
18 
revenue requirement. 
19

rates and revenues, and simplicity and understandability.

2 
based on “gross” or “net” load. A gross load construct would apply transmission 
3 
charges to the load-only portion of the co-located customer, while a net load 
4 
construct would subtract any generation from the load before applying charges. A 
5 
net load construct is consistent with measuring the actual energy flowing between 
6 
the entire co-location configuration and the transmission system as demonstrated 
7 
in the figure below. These concepts are discussed in more detail in later sections of

my testimony.

Q12. PLEASE 
PROVIDE 
AN 
OVERVIEW 
OF 
WHAT 
CAUSES 
12 
TRANSMISSION COSTS. 
13 
A12. Transmission is built to allow for delivery of generation to loads. The sizing of the 
14 
transmission grid is primarily determined by the need to deliver generation to loads 
15

11 
during peak demand. In its Electric Utility Cost Allocation Manuel, the National 
1 
Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (“NARUC”) states that 
2 
“investment in the transmission system is generally assumed to be driven by 
3 
increments in system peak load.” 16 FERC has similarly acknowledged this in 
4 
multiple ratemaking decisions; for instance, while defending a peak load-based 
5 
transmission cost allocation in Docket No. EL00-66-000, FERC stated that:  
6 
“A utility builds its bulk power facilities, i.e., generating units and transmission 
7 
lines, to meet the maximum or peak demand of its firm customers. Because the 
8 
utility incurs the cost of these facilities to meet the peak demand of its firm 
9 
customers, those customers should pay for the facilities. The peak responsibility 
10 
method accomplishes this by allocating the cost of the facilities among the firm 
11 
customers in the same proportion as each customer's demand bears to the system 
12 
peak.”17 
13 
From this first principle, it naturally follows that the integration of new 
14 
loads within an electricity system in a manner that does not increase peak demand 
15 
will result in lower transmission system costs than integration of new loads that do 
16 
increase peak demand. This notion is also well-supported in literature – for 
17 
example, a recent study authored by researchers at Duke University states that “[t]o 
18 
the extent a new load can temporarily reduce (i.e., curtail) its electricity 
19 
consumption from the grid during these peak stress periods, however, it may be 
20 
able to connect while deferring—or even avoiding—the need for certain 
21 
upgrades.”18 
22

Q13. HOW DOES THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN PEAK DEMAND AND 
1 
TRANSMISSION COSTS IMPACT RATE DESIGN? 
2 
A13. The fact that transmission costs are incurred by a need to serve peak demand is the 
3 
basis for demand charges, which are the industry-standard approach to recovering 
4 
transmission costs across the U.S. 19  Customers with higher coincident peak 
5 
demands20 on the transmission system cause a higher portion of total system costs 
6 
and are therefore allocated a higher share of total system costs. In PJM, the Network 
7 
Service Peak Load metric represents a customer’s contribution to peak load of the 
8 
transmission system and is used to allocate transmission service charges for 
9 
customers that take Network Service.21  
10 
The fact that these demand charges are nearly universal in the industry to 
11 
recover transmission costs is a direct reflection of the relationship between 
12 
transmission costs and peak demand. Put differently, if the size of a customer’s load 
13 
on the transmission system during the system peak were not indicative of the costs 
14 
this customer caused, then there would be no basis for differentiating charges based 
15 
on the size of a customer’s peak load. 
16 
 
19 https://pubs.naruc.org/pub.cfm?id=5378847A-2354-D714-5165-3DDAA31643D2. 
20 Coincident peak demand is defined as a customer’s demand during the system peak. 
21 https://www.pjm.com/markets-and-operations/billing-settlements-and-credit/guide-to-billing.

Q14. CAN THE COST ASSOCIATED WITH EXPANSION OF THE 
1 
TRANSMISSION SYSTEM TO MEET INCREASES IN PEAK DEMAND 
2 
BE QUANTIFIED? 
3 
A14. Yes. The impact on transmission costs from peak load increases is quantified 
4 
through marginal cost analysis. 22  These methods quantify transmission cost 
5 
increases ($) for a given increase in peak load (MW), resulting in a $/MW value. 
6 
Similarly, avoiding or deferring an increase in peak load reduces transmission 
7 
system costs.  
8

9 
A15. Transmission marginal cost values are used in a multitude of ways in the industry, 
10 
including system planning, cost allocation, rate design, program compensation, and 
11 
more. 23 Another notable use of marginal costs is to quantify the benefits of 
12 
distributed energy resources, including energy efficiency, demand response, and 
13 
distributed generation. 24  These values are used to set program incentives, 
14 
compensation structures, and more.  
15

Q16. CAN EFFECTIVE RATE DESIGN ENABLE TRANSMISSION SYSTEM 
1 
COST REDUCTIONS? 
2 
A16. Yes. Developing rate designs in which costs incurred by customers mirror the costs 
3 
that are being imposed (or avoided) on the transmission system incentivizes loads 
4 
(and, similarly, distributed energy resources) to engage in behavior that reduces the 
5 
peak load on the transmission system – for example by shifting load, participating 
6 
in demand response, investing in energy efficiency, investing in distributed 
7 
generation, co-locating loads and generation, and more. 
8 
Q17. WHY IS INCENTIVIZING THIS BEHAVIOR BENEFICIAL? 
9 
A17. Without incentivizing behavior to reduce the system peak, this beneficial behavior 
10 
would simply not happen. This well-established concept has encouraged 
11 
policymakers to implement rate structures and designs precisely to incentivize 
12 
changes in behavior, recognizing that without price signals, loads have no incentive 
13 
to act in ways that reduces system costs.25 
14 
Q18. WHAT ARE THE IMPACTS OF REDUCING SYSTEM COSTS? 
15 
A18. Utilities recover their total revenue requirement from customers – a well-
16 
established rate design principle. Therefore, reducing the total revenue requirement 
17 
has the impact of reducing total customer costs and improving affordability.  
18

2023.pdf.

Q19. PLEASE DEFINE “CO-LOCATED LOAD.” 
1 
A19. “Co-located load” refers to an electrical load that is electrically connected behind 
2 
the same point of interconnection as a generator, enabling it to be served directly 
3 
by the generator without the associated energy flowing over the transmission 
4 
system. An illustration of a standard load and co-located load configuration is 
5 
provided in the figure below. 
6

Q20. ARE THERE DIFFERENT POTENTIAL CONFIGURATIONS OF CO-
9 
LOCATED LOADS WITH DIFFERENT TRANSMISSION SYSTEM 
10 
IMPACTS? 
11 
A20. Yes. There are a range of different potential configurations for co-located loads that 
12 
impact the transmission system differently. Broadly speaking, these can be 
13 
organized into three fundamental configurations of co-located load: 
14 
• Firm: This represents a co-located load configuration that uses co-located 
15 
generation when it is available but has the right to draw from the grid when 
16 
the co-located generation is not available. 
17

16 
• Generator-contingent: This represents a configuration where co-located 
1 
load uses co-located generation when it is available but has no right to draw 
2 
from the grid when it is not. In other words, if the co-located generator is 
3 
available, the co-located load cannot be interrupted. However, if the co-
4 
located generator is not available, the co-located load can be interrupted. 
5 
Therefore, the co-located load is contingent on the availability of the 
6 
generator. 
7 
• Interruptible: This represents a configuration where co-located load can 
8 
be interrupted by PJM at any time, regardless of whether the co-located 
9 
generator is online and available. Interruptions may be facilitated through 
10 
either load curtailment or additional backup generation, but it must be 
11 
enforceable and long-duration. This means that PJM must be certain that 
12 
the co-located load will interrupt whenever system conditions require 
13 
without any limit applied to the length of the interruption.  
14 
 
15 
Both the “generator-contingent” and “interruptible” configurations can be 
16 
designed such that the co-located load can draw energy from the transmission 
17 
system on an as-available basis.  
18 
Q21. HOW DO THESE DIFFERENT POTENTIAL CONFIGURATIONS 
19 
IMPACT TRANSMISSION SYSTEM COSTS? 
20 
A21. The impact of a co-located load on the transmission system and corresponding costs 
21 
depends on its configuration. PJM acknowledges this in its statement that 
22 
“incremental load gives rise to incremental system costs. But the extent of those 
23

17 
costs appears to vary based on the nature of the particular co-location 
1 
arrangement.”26 For any potential co-location configuration, cost impacts to the 
2 
transmission system are driven by the impact on grid power flows primarily during 
3 
the system peak. Different configurations have different transmission system 
4 
impacts:  
5 
• Firm: Under this configuration, the transmission system must be planned 
6 
and built to serve the co-located load, even if on-site generation is not 
7 
available. At the same time, it is not necessary to plan and build the 
8 
transmission system to serve the entirety of all co-located load, as the 
9 
natural diversity of loads and resources across the system make it 
10 
implausible that all co-located generation will be unavailable at the same 
11 
time (just as it is implausible that all PJM generation will be unavailable). 
12 
Using statistical methods that account for generator outage diversity, 
13 
planners can calculate the aggregate contribution toward the system peak 
14 
and corresponding transmission system requirements for firm loads with co-
15 
located or behind-the-meter generation. 
16 
• Generator-contingent: Under this configuration, the transmission system 
17 
does not need to be sized to serve the co-located load during the peak period, 
18 
as the load is dependent on the on-site generator for supply and is not 
19 
entitled to be served from the grid when the generator is not available. At 
20 
the same time, the addition of co-located load in this configuration may 
21 
impact power flows that could potentially overload parts of the system, 
22

18 
meaning that transmission upgrades may still be necessary to ensure the 
1 
reliability of the system. 
2 
However, if the co-located load in this configuration is added in 
3 
certain areas of the transmission system (such as a local generation pocket 
4 
that requires exporting electricity) or in conjunction with an increase in 
5 
generation, there may be minimal if any required transmission system 
6 
upgrades. In fact, these co-located loads may even reduce potential 
7 
transmission system overloads and future potential upgrades.27 
8 
• Interruptible: Under this configuration, because PJM has the ability to 
9 
interrupt the co-located load to ensure transmission system reliability, there 
10 
is minimal, if any, impact to transmission system costs.28 
11 
 
12 
For any energy that is withdrawn on an “as-available” basis in the 
13 
“generator-contingent” or “interruptible” configuration, this energy would only be 
14 
provided if the transmission system, as built, is capable of delivering it. This would 
15 
therefore not require any additional investment in transmission infrastructure.

1 
Q22. HOW DOES THE CURRENT PJM TRANSMISSION TARIFF APPLY TO 
2 
CO-LOCATED LOADS? 
3 
A22. The current tariff does not provide sufficient clarity on how co-located loads should 
4 
be charged for transmission service, resulting in different interpretations and 
5 
applications of the tariff by different transmission owners within PJM. Several 
6 
transmission owners have interpreted the tariff as requiring all loads (co-located or 
7 
not) to be served under NITS, take firm service, and pay for transmission service 
8 
based on their full gross load, even if no electricity is being withdrawn from the 
9 
transmission system. For example, in its proposed revisions to its Open Access 
10 
Transmission Tariff (“OATT”), Exelon—through Atlantic City Electric 
11 
Company—states that “[s]ervice to such co-located load is Network Integration 
12 
Transmission Service (“NITS”) as defined in the PJM OATT.” 29  Other 
13 
transmission owners have interpreted the tariff as allowing co-located 
14 
configurations. For example, PSE&G has stated that “data centers should have the 
15 
option to select a configuration that best fits their particular circumstances and 
16 
needs – whether this is in front of the meter or a co-location arrangement.”30 PPL 
17 
also supported a co-location arrangement without requiring the co-located load to 
18 
take NITS service; in their proposed Interconnection Service Agreement (“ISA”) 
19 
with Susquehanna Nuclear, LLC, PPL states that “[t]he Co-Located Load is not 
20

20 
Network Load, and it is intended that the Co-Located Load will never consume 
1 
capacity and/or energy from the PJM Transmission System, including the 
2 
Interconnected Transmission Owner’s transmission facilities.”31 Even PJM until 
3 
recently supported the notion that “[c]o-located must either be PJM Network Load 
4 
(with applicable firm transmission service or not PJM Network Load (load without 
5 
applicable firm transmission service.”32

Q23. IS THE TARIFF’S LACK OF CLARITY ALIGNED WITH RATE DESIGN 
7 
PRINCIPLES? 
8 
A23. No. One of Bonbright’s foundational rate design principles states that rates should 
9 
be “free from controversies as to improper interpretation.”33 The fact that different 
10 
transmission owners are interpreting the tariff differently is an obvious indicator of 
11 
the ambiguity of the existing tariff. Additionally, Bonbright states that rates should 
12 
be “non-discriminatory.” The fact that the possibility exists that some co-located 
13 
loads may be charged for transmission based on their gross behind-the-meter load 
14 
while others may be charged based on net withdrawal from the transmission system 
15 
purely based on the local transmission owner’s tariff interpretation is unduly 
16 
discriminatory and not aligned with this principle.  
17 
Q24. CONSIDERING THE AMBIGUITY PRESENT IN THE CURRENT 
18 
TARIFF, IS THE INTERPRETATION THAT REQUIRES CO-LOCATED 
19 
LOAD TO TAKE NITS SERVICE AND PAY TRANSMISSION CHARGES 
20 
 
31 Susquehanna ISA Amended, page 106, Docket No. ER24-2172-000. 
32 Page 4, https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/pjm-guidance-on-co-
located-load.pdf. 
33 James C. Bonbright, Principles of Public Utility Rates, page 291.

21 
BASED ON GROSS LOAD ALIGNED WITH PRECEDENT AND 
1 
TREATMENT OF OTHER LOADS IN PJM? 
2 
A24. No. Requiring all load to be served under NITS (or Point-to-Point service) and 
3 
assessing charges based on gross load is inconsistent with treatment of other loads 
4 
in PJM. Neither PJM nor any of its transmission owners (including the ones that 
5 
assert above that co-located load is network load) require full NITS service for load 
6 
served directly by behind-the-meter generation, whose transmission charges are 
7 
determined based on their net load served by the transmission system. 34 This 
8
